sb26:
MECHANICAL FACTS (measured offline against the live game, not guessed):

  SUBMIT IS action 5. This is the single most important fact about this game.
  Arranging the pieces correctly does NOT complete a level. Nothing happens until you
  press(5). Verified by experiment: with level 1 arranged correctly, press(7) does not
  clear it and a stray click does not clear it, but press(5) clears it immediately.
  Six earlier runs arranged the board perfectly, saw no completion, concluded the order
  must be wrong, and burned thousands of actions permuting a board that was already
  right. If you have placed every piece and nothing happened, press(5) BEFORE you
  change anything.

  DRAG AND DROP: click a tray piece to pick it up, then click a destination pad to drop
  it. Clicking a destination alone does nothing.

  BOARD LAYOUT, every level so far:
    top row (y~3): the CLUE row. Each clue is a 20px ring of the target colour with a
      16px c5 square inside it. Read the clues left to right by cx; that is the order.
    middle (15 < y < 50): the destination PADS, small 4px c2 dots. Level 1 has one row
      of them. Level 2 has two rows (y~22 and y~36), so pad reading order is a real
      question there, not an afterthought.
    bottom row (y~58): the TRAY, 16px squares, one per piece, in scrambled order.

  THE ROW-53 BAR IS A TIMER. A c2 bar spans row 53 and a c3 segment eats it from the
  right as ticks pass. It is not scenery and it is not a piece. When it runs out you
  die. This is why long permutation searches produced dozens of deaths: the cost was
  not just wasted actions, it was running the clock out over and over.

  grid() IS STALE FOR ONE FRAME after a level change. The first read on a new level can
  still show the old board. Spend one action, then re-read before you trust coordinates.

  Level 1 solves in 9 actions: 4 pick/drop pairs in clue order, then press(5).

  ACTION 7 IS UNDO, and it only does anything from level 2 on. On level 1 it is inert.
  With pieces on the board, each press(7) sends the most recently placed piece back to
  the tray, last in first out. Measured: six presses removed six pieces one at a time,
  bottom row first because that was the placement order. Use it to correct a single
  misplacement instead of rebuilding, but remember every press costs an action.

  LEVEL 2, SOLVED. Verified offline by exhaustive search at no score cost. It has 7
  clues [12,15,8,9,14,11,6], 7 tray pieces and 7 c2 pads: three at y=22 (x 22,28,40) and
  four at y=36 (x 22,28,34,40). The top row SKIPS x=34; the bottom row has it. The
  winning assignment is:
    (22,22)=12  (28,22)=15  (40,22)=6
    (22,36)=8   (28,36)=9   (34,36)=14  (40,36)=11
  Read against the clue row that is raster order with one twist: clues 1 and 2 go to the
  first two top pads, clues 3-6 fill the whole bottom row left to right, and the LAST
  clue goes to the top-right pad. The gap at top x=34 pushes that pad to the end of the
  path. This is why the obvious answer fails: the split is 2 on top and 5 below, not 3
  and 4. All 144 arrangements that keep 3 on top and 4 below were built, verified and
  submitted offline, and every one was rejected.
  Solve it in 15 actions: seven pick/drop pairs in the assignment above, then press(5).
  Do not permute. The space was already searched exhaustively; the answer is above.

  ACTION 7 IS UNDO, and it only does anything from level 2 on. On level 1 it is inert.
  With pieces on the board, each press(7) sends the most recently placed piece back to
  the tray, last in first out. Measured: six presses removed six pieces one at a time.
  Use it to correct a single misplacement instead of rebuilding, but it costs an action.

  PLACEMENT ORDER DOES NOT MATTER. The board is scored as a MAPPING -- which colour ends
  up on which pad -- and not as a path through the pads. Measured offline against the live
  game: a winning assignment for level 3, level 4 and level 5 was replayed with the
  placement sequence randomly shuffled, three shuffles each, and all nine cleared.
  This matters because searching over traversal orders searches a space that is factorially
  too large and almost entirely made of duplicates: two different 'routes' that put the same
  colour on the same pad ARE THE SAME ANSWER and the board cannot tell them apart. A measured
  run spent thirteen turns and a million tokens on level 5 and tested only three distinct
  assignments, because it was reasoning about the order to walk the pads in.
  Ask WHICH CLUE BELONGS ON WHICH PAD. Do not ask in what order to walk them.
  Testing one assignment costs about 2N+1 actions -- 17 on a seven-piece board. That is
  cheap next to the action budget, but the row-53 timer still runs, so think before each
  test and make each one rule out a family of answers rather than a single arrangement.

  THE CLUE ROW IS NOT ALWAYS A FLAT ONE-RING-PER-PIECE LIST. Measured on level 5: the row
  draws NINE rings while the tray holds EIGHT pieces, and the two do not even agree as
  multisets -- rings are {6, 8x4, 11, 14x2, 15} against a tray of {6, 8x2, 9x2, 11, 14, 15}.
  Level 6 by contrast is a clean 1:1, so you cannot assume either shape; check.
  When the clue count does not equal the pad count, the row is telling you it has
  STRUCTURE: some rings do not stand for one piece each. Measured failure mode, three runs
  in a row: the agent wrote `assert len(clues) == len(pads) == len(tray)`, crashed, and
  spent the rest of the level guessing assignments instead of reading the row.
  When they disagree, look at the row as drawn -- the sequence of ring colours left to
  right, repeated blocks within it, and which of those colours are also FRAME colours
  rather than tray colours. A colour that names a frame is unlikely to be naming a piece.

  LEVELS 5-8 ARE UNEXPLORED. Expect the same verbs (click to pick, click a pad to drop,
  5 to submit, 7 to undo) and a layout you must read fresh with objects(). Do not assume
  level 2's coordinates or its ordering twist carry over.
